pr_body:
coredump: check cgroups memory limit if storing on tmpfs
    
When /var/lib/systemd/coredump/ is backed by a tmpfs, all disk usage
will be accounted under the systemd-coredump process cgroup memory
limit.
If MemoryMax is set, this might cause systemd-coredump to be terminated
by the kernel oom handler when writing large uncompressed core files,
even if the compressed core would fit within the limits.

Detect if a tmpfs is used, and if so check MemoryMax from the process
and slice cgroups, and do not write uncompressed core files that are
greater than half the available memory. If the limit is breached,
stop writing and compress the written chunk immediately, then delete
the uncompressed chunk to free more memory, and resume compressing
directly from STDIN.

Example debug log when this situation happens:

```
systemd-coredump[737455]: Setting max_size to limit writes to 51344896 bytes.
systemd-coredump[737455]: ZSTD compression finished (51344896 -> 3260 bytes, 0.0%)
systemd-coredump[737455]: ZSTD compression finished (1022786048 -> 47245 bytes, 0.0%)
systemd-coredump[737455]: Process 737445 (a.out) of user 1000 dumped core.
```

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/13968
pr_comments: (i understand that some of the size_t type confusion is a pre-existing issue. Generally, we should use size_t for things in memory and uint64_t for things on disk. Thus, when compressing/decompressing we can should use size_t for the file fragment of data currently in memory, and use uint64_t for the overall file size)

> This patch assumes that the cgroup memory limits apply to files that processes write to tmpfs. Is this really correct? @htejun is this true, are writes to tmpfs charged against memory use by memcg?

Yes, this is correct.

> @htejun this patch adds a new D-Bus property MemoryAvailable that returns the effective "available" memory for a cgroup, which is defined done by subtracting the MemoryUsage value of each unit from the MemoryMax value, starting from the relevant cgroup, going up the tree for each slice. The hierarchy walk makes sense, but the cgroup configurations could use either high or max to limit available memory. The calculation for this purpose here should use whichever is more restrictive.

But other than that, the overall feature makes sense to me.

issue_context.title: Please support on-the-fly compression of core dumps
issue_context.body:
Some runtimes and libraries allocate a huge address space on startup, even if they use only a small fraction of it later. Dumping core of such applications is unnecessarily resource intensive, because even though such core files compress very well with little effort, systemd-coredump first writes the uncompressed image to be able to log the backtrace (I guess), and only then compresses the file. This requires great temporarily filesystem capacity and entails much wasted I/O. I think this automatic analysis is rather superficial and the admin either won't care or will have to redo it anyway in most of the cases. On another system, because the necessary software and resources may not even be available on the problem system. Unless the capacity requirement denied the creation of the core file to start with... even the default 2 GB may not be available on some systems, but the compressed core would fit easily.

I'd like to have the option of forgoing this automatic backtrace generation and any other analysis in exchange of on-the-fly core compression. This would also speed up dumping considerably by not writing the uncompressed data (which is removed short after anyway).

Otherwise I'll have to resort to using a home-grown compression script as my `core_pattern`, resulting in unnecessary non-uniformity amongst our servers.
comments: hmm, if this is desirable it should probably have an automatism that we first try to write and process it like we now do, but if we notice it grows too large while doing so, we switch to off processing, compress what we already have and then write the rest only compressed. i.e. be nice when we can, and if we can't then handle that too. Would be one more size threshold to configure in coredump.conf.
I am tinkering with coredump these days. Turns out you can get ridiculous savings when writing sparse files (1.2GB vs 60MB uncompressed). Should be rather easy to do.

I am working on this. First part is a fix for the LZ4 compressor: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/18941
Once that is merged after 248 is out, I'll follow-up with this which changes core handling to first use the STDIN FD to stream compress, and then if possible decompress+load for backtrace generation: https://github.com/bluca/systemd/commits/coredump_compress_on_the_fly
